newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK interim assembly should quit soon--party chief.
newsitem.headline: HK interim assembly should quit soon--party chief.

text.p: Hong Kong's shadow Provisional Legislature lacks credibility because it is not popularly elected and should dissolve itself as soon as possible, pro-China Liberal Party leader Allen Lee said on Friday.
This interim parliament, taking over when Britain gives Hong Kong back to China in 11 days' time, has been widely criticised by pro-democracy lobbyists here and Western states.

Lee sits in both Hong Kong's existing Legislative Council, a body widely viewed as democratic because half of its members are popularly elected, and in the Provisional Legislature, appointed by 400 people hand-picked by Beijing.
"The earlier we dissolve this controversy of having the Provisional Legislature the better," Lee told reporters at a news conference at Hong Kong's Foreign Correspondents' Club.
"I'm not surprised the level of (public) support is very low...it is because it is not popularly elected."
The Legislative Council will expire at midnight on June 30 when the handover of power ends a colonial interlude of more than 150 years.
The Provisional Legislature, which has been meeting across the border in China, will then become Hong Kong's official law-making body.
Lee said he would prefer the Provisional Legislature to dissolve in January 1998 after passing a new law on elections but doubted that would be possible because of a need for a March budget.
He set April 1998 as the soonest likely date for dissolution.
Controversy over Beijing's decision to replace Hong Kong's Legislative Council with the Provisional Legislature has been the biggest bump in the road to transfer of power.
Britain introduced democratic reforms to Hong Kong only after the date for a handover of the territory had been agreed.
Lee said he worried about the possibility of future corruption, both on the Chinese mainland and in Hong Kong.

Lee said Hong Kong's Chief Executive-designate, Tung Chee-hwa, should be prepared for telephone calls from mainland officials trying to influence events in Hong Kong, which by agreement is supposed to maintain manage its own affairs for 50 years.
"He will get his phone calls. (The question is) how's he going to manage Hong Kong, how's he going to run Hong Kong?" Lee said.
"People will look upon him to defend Hong Kong's interests. That is his most important job."

Asked about Hong Kong's skyrocketing property prices and unsatisfied housing demand, Allen Lee laid much of the blame on speculators and the Hong Kong government, which he said had artificially inflated prices on public land sales.
Lee indicated his Liberal Party would support anti-speculative legislation but not a capital gains tax on property transactions, which he said would "open up another can of worms".
